steps.tx: Serum **TSH** measurement serves as the definitive initial screening test for primary thyroid disorders in ambulatory patients with an intact hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid axis. Because pituitary thyrotrophs respond logarithmically to minute shifts in circulating thyroid hormones, TSH detects incipient primary dysfunction with exceptional sensitivity. However, when evaluating suspected **central hypothyroidism** due to sellar pathology, TSH loses screening validity, necessitating direct measurement of **free T4**.
steps.say: Serum TSH is the first-line screening investigation for primary thyroid disorders when pituitary function is intact. Because thyrotrophs respond exponentially to small variations in hormone levels, TSH is highly sensitive. In suspected central hypothyroidism, however, clinicians must measure free T4 directly because TSH values may be falsely normal.

steps.tx: The **Wolff-Chaikoff effect** describes an acute, autoregulatory shutdown of thyroid hormone organification and follicular synthesis following exposure to an acute intrathyroidal iodine excess. In healthy individuals, the thyroid gland escapes from this organification block within 10 to 14 days by down-regulating sodium-iodide symporter expression. Conversely, in patients with underlying autonomous nodular goitre, excess iodine administration may provoke autonomous hyperthyroidism, termed the **Jod-Basedow effect**.
steps.say: The Wolff-Chaikoff effect is a transient autoregulatory arrest of thyroid hormone organification in response to acute iodine excess. Healthy thyroid tissue can overcome this inhibition after ten to fourteen days. In contrast, patients with autonomous multinodular goitre exposed to excess iodine can develop severe thyrotoxicosis, known as the Jod-Basedow phenomenon.

left.title: Wolff-Chaikoff Effect
points: Transient inhibition of thyroid peroxidase organification
Utilized therapeutically in thyroid storm preparation

right.title: Jod-Basedow Effect
points: Iodine exposure in multinodular or latent Graves

steps.tx: Over 80% of circulating active triiodothyronine derives from the extrathyroidal 5-prime monodeiodination of thyroxine mediated by peripheral **deiodinases**, primarily type 1 and type 2 enzymes. In acute critical systemic disease, down-regulation of peripheral deiodinases produces the **nonthyroidal illness** syndrome, characterized by low serum total and free T3, normal or low TSH, and a compensatory rise in biologically inactive **reverse T3** generated by type 3 inner-ring deiodinase.
steps.say: Most circulating triiodothyronine is produced by peripheral outer-ring deiodination of thyroxine by deiodinases. During critical medical illness, deiodinase activity shifts, causing low circulating T3, normal or low TSH, and elevated reverse T3. This nonthyroidal illness syndrome should not be treated with thyroid hormone replacement.

steps.tx: Gestational estrogen surges and oral contraceptive therapy stimulate hepatic glycosylation and prolong the clearance of **thyroid-binding globulin**, substantially increasing total circulating concentrations of **total T4**. However, homeostatic negative feedback maintains normal physiological free thyroxine concentrations throughout gestation. Consequently, total hormone assays must be interpreted using gestational trimester-specific reference ranges or replaced entirely by validated free thyroxine immunoassays.
steps.say: High circulating estrogen during pregnancy elevates hepatic thyroid-binding globulin synthesis and increases total thyroxine. Negative feedback keeps euthyroid free hormone concentrations in balance. Clinicians must rely on trimester-specific reference ranges or direct free thyroxine measurements rather than total hormone assays.

steps.tx: The physiological plasma **half-life** of **levothyroxine** is approximately 7 days, whereas synthetic **liothyronine** exhibits a significantly shorter elimination half-life of roughly 24 hours. Because steady-state equilibrium requires approximately five half-lives, adjustments in oral levothyroxine dosing should be evaluated with follow-up serum TSH testing no sooner than 6 to 8 weeks after any dose modification, avoiding premature and misleading dose titrations.
steps.say: Levothyroxine has an elimination half-life of seven days, whereas liothyronine has a half-life of only one day. Because reaching pharmacokinetic steady state requires five half-lives, clinicians should reassess serum TSH six to eight weeks after changing the levothyroxine dose, rather than titrating too early.

left.title: Levothyroxine (T4)
points: Acts as a prohormone converted peripherally
Requires 6 to 8 weeks to assess steady-state TSH

right.title: Liothyronine (T3)
points: Rapid onset used in myxoedema coma protocols

steps.tx: High-dose over-the-counter **biotin** supplementation, frequently consumed for hair and nail health, causes profound analytical interference in commercial streptavidin-biotinylated immunoassays. Biotin displaces assay reagents, falsely producing elevated **free T4** and spuriously suppressed **TSH**, thereby masquerading as primary biochemical thyrotoxicosis. Clinicians must advise patients to discontinue biotin supplements for at least 48 to 72 hours before elective thyroid testing.
steps.say: High-dose biotin supplements interfere with streptavidin-biotin immunoassay platforms, causing falsely elevated free T4 and spuriously suppressed TSH. This biochemical artefact imitates Graves disease. Patients must stop taking biotin for at least forty-eight to seventy-two hours before elective thyroid function testing.

steps.tx: The biochemical finding of **subclinical thyrotoxicosis** is characterized by a persistently suppressed serum **TSH** concentration in the presence of strictly normal circulating free T4 and free T3 levels. Grade 1 subclinical thyrotoxicosis features a TSH between 0.1 and 0.4 mIU/L, whereas Grade 2 features a TSH below 0.1 mIU/L. Grade 2 confers an elevated long-term risk of developing **atrial fibrillation**, osteoporosis, and fracture.
steps.say: Subclinical thyrotoxicosis is defined as a suppressed TSH with normal circulating free T4 and T3 concentrations. Grade 2 suppression with TSH below 0.1 mIU per litre significantly increases the long-term risk of atrial fibrillation, osteopenia, and cardiovascular mortality, warranting definitive treatment in older adults.

rows: Low adverse risk; observe or treat if >65 years
High risk of atrial fibrillation; treat definitively

steps.tx: The class III antiarrhythmic agent **amiodarone** contains 37% iodine by weight and exerts complex effects on the thyroid gland, including inhibition of type 1 deiodinase. Amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis is classified into type 1, an iodine-induced hyperthyroidism occurring in abnormal glands treated with thionamides, and type 2, a destructive thyroiditis managed with corticosteroids. Baseline and surveillance serum **TSH** must be checked prior to initiation and every 6 months.
steps.say: Amiodarone contains significant iodine and inhibits peripheral deiodinases. It can cause either iodine-induced hyperthyroidism in abnormal glands, known as type 1, or destructive thyroiditis in normal glands, known as type 2. Baseline and regular six-monthly TSH monitoring is mandatory during long-term therapy.

left.title: Amiodarone Type 1
points: Pre-existing multinodular goitre or latent Graves
Colour Doppler shows normal or increased flow

right.title: Amiodarone Type 2
points: Occurs in anatomically normal thyroid glands
Colour Doppler shows absent vascular flow
Treated with oral corticosteroids such as prednisolone
